nameStory: The Amber Glass snail gets its name from its shell's stunning translucent appearance that looks exactly like a piece of polished amber or golden glass. When light passes through the thin shell, it glows with a warm, honey-colored radiance that's unmistakable once you've seen it.
description: The Amber Glass is a tiny land snail with one of the most beautiful shells you'll find in New England. This diminutive mollusk measures only about 3-4 millimeters across—smaller than a pencil eraser. Its low, flattened spiral shell is so thin and translucent that it appears to be made of golden glass, giving you a peek at the snail's soft body inside. Despite its delicate appearance, this little snail is surprisingly hardy and can be found in various woodland habitats.

idTips.label: Translucent amber shell
idTips.description: The shell is remarkably see-through with a golden-amber color that glows when backlit, feeling paper-thin and smooth to the touch

idTips.label: Tiny size
idTips.description: Measures only 3-4mm across—about the size of a small ant or the tip of a ballpoint pen

idTips.label: Flattened coil shape
idTips.description: Shell is noticeably low and wide rather than tall, with a gentle spiral that feels smooth under your fingertip

idTips.label: Glossy surface
idTips.description: Shell has a polished, glass-like shine that reflects light and feels slippery when slightly damp

idTips.label: Visible body through shell
idTips.description: The snail's dark soft body is clearly visible through the transparent shell, creating interesting shadow patterns

habitat: Look for Amber Glass snails in moist deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly under rotting logs, leaf litter, and mossy areas. They prefer spots with rich, organic soil and consistent moisture, often hiding beneath fallen maple, oak, or birch leaves. These snails are most common in lowland to mid-elevation forests where the soil stays damp but not waterlogged.

seasonality.spring: Active snails emerge as snow melts, often found crawling on damp leaf litter in early morning. This is prime time to spot them before vegetation gets too thick.
seasonality.summer: During dry spells, snails retreat deep into leaf litter and under logs where they're harder to find. Early morning after rain showers offers the best viewing opportunities.
seasonality.fall: Peak activity returns as moisture increases and temperatures cool. Fresh leaf fall provides excellent hunting grounds as snails feed on decomposing organic matter.
seasonality.winter: Snails hibernate deep in soil or under thick leaf litter. Empty shells may occasionally be found on the surface after winter storms.

funFact: The Amber Glass snail's shell is so thin that scientists can actually watch its heart beating through the translucent walls—it's like having a living, crawling window into snail anatomy!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small glass snails in the family, but the warm amber color and extremely small size set it apart from clearer or larger species. Remember: if it glows golden like honey when you hold it up to the light, you've found your Amber Glass.
compareHints: Since Amber Glass is the only Perpolita species commonly found in New England, compare it to other members of the Gastrodontidae family like Nesovitrea or Zonitoides species. Amber Glass is distinguished by its smaller size and distinctly golden-amber coloration, while related glass snails tend to be either larger, clearer, or have different shell proportions.
